newsitem.title: UK: Worldwide advertising spending seen up 4.2 pct.
newsitem.headline: Worldwide advertising spending seen up 4.2 pct.

text.p: Worldwide spending on advertising is projected to increase 4.2 percent in 1996, but growth in the following three years is expected to be less robust, a leading media buying and planning group said on Tuesday.

"Global adspend in print, TV, radio and cinema and out-of-home is forecast to be $291 billion in 1996, 7.8 percent ahead of 1995 in current prices or 4.2 percent in constant (prices)," Zenith Media said in its annual Advertising Expenditure Forecast.

"We continue to forecast 1996 to be the high point of real growth to 1999, though real annual forecast growth rates are up about 0.5 percent in the light of steady economic fundamentals and rising consumption, particularly in the U.S.," Zenith said.
Zenith is a unit of Cordiant Plc, the advertising and marketing group which includes the Saatchi & Saatchi and Bates Dorland advertising agencies.

Worldwide advertising expenditure totalled $270.5 billion in 1995, including $99.5 billion from North America, $77.3 billion from Europe, $70.5 billion from Asia/Pacific, $18.3 billion from Latin America, and $4.8 billion from Africa and the Middle East.

At constant prices, Zenith said it expected the global advertising market to increase 4.2 percent in 1996, 3.2 percent in 1997, 2.7 percent in 1998 and 2.9 percent in 1999. Asia/Pacific is seen contributing the strongest growth, forecast at 7.7 percent in constant prices in 1996, 5.9 percent in 1997, 4.4 percent in 1998 and 5.0 percent in 1999.

North America and Europe, by contrast, will have more modest growth. Zenith said it sees growth in North America at 3.0 percent in 1996, 1.7 percent in 1997, 1.6 percent in 1998 and 1.3 percent in 1999. In Europe Zenith forecasts growth at 2.6 percent in 1996, 2.5 percent in 1997, 2.3 percent in 1998 and 2.9 percent in 1999.

Television became the largest single advertising medium in the U.S. in 1995, overtaking newspapers for the first time. Television accounted for $35.7 billion in advertising revenues versus $35.3 billion for newspapers. Both media claimed a 37 percent share of the U.S. advertising market in 1995.
"By 1999 we place TV at 40 percent of major media spend and newspapers at 36 percent," Zenith said. "Cable is a key driver, with revenues rising 15 percent every year as it builds audience share."
An expected settlement in 1997 of terms for the planned European Monetary Union should remove uncertainty and liberate some advertising demand in Europe, Zenith said.

Europe continues to have a low rate of advertising spending in proportion to gross domestic product at 0.86 percent, reflecting the widespread existence of non-commercial television and high rates. In Europe television claims 30 percent of the total advertising market.
Latin America is the world's largest user of media in relation to GDP, at 1.29 percent, and Latin American advertisers are proportionately the world's heaviest users of television, Zenith said.

Zenith said it had trimmed its advertising spending outlook for Latin America by two percentage points for 1996/97, reflecting doubts about the political stamina needed to maintain economic recovery and reform. "Looking out to 1998/1999, the region gets the benfit of the doubt and returns to the longterm low-teens trend rate previously forecast," Zenith said.
